threads.body: The new guidance says to set `error.type` on server spans for timeouts/transport errors, but the surrounding note also says `error.type` SHOULD be set to the JSON-RPC error code string “if one is returned”. For timeouts/transport errors there is no JSON-RPC error code, so the spec should explicitly state what `error.type` value to use in that case (e.g., `timeout` or exception type), to avoid conflicting/ambiguous normative guidance.

Parking my notes on the PR description here.

- The description lists the four JSON-RPC pre-defined client codes, but MCP also defines `-32002` (`Resource not found`) — the canonical "not found" case the motivation calls out. It falls in the `-32000`..`-32099` range this PR classifies as a *server* error, so it still gets reported as a server-side failure. Details in my comment on `model/mcp/spans.yaml`.
- "Reference scenarios updated for affected libraries" is unchecked. There are no MCP scenarios under `reference/scenarios/` today (nothing emits `mcp.method.name`), so it's N/A — worth saying so in the description so nobody blocks on it.
- The fragment only describes the server-side half. The PR also newly defines the client-side classification ("All JSON-RPC error codes SHOULD be considered errors") and splits `error.type` guidance by client/server, which consumers will want to know about.

```suggestion
Clarify MCP error reporting: MCP server telemetry no longer reports client-side JSON-RPC errors (parse errors, invalid requests, method not found, and invalid params) as failures, while MCP client telemetry reports all JSON-RPC error codes as errors.
```

Two issues with this requirement level.

**"spans" leaks into the metric tables.** `mcp.common.attributes` is also pulled in by `mcp.operation.metrics.attributes`, so this text renders verbatim into the `mcp.client.operation.duration` and `mcp.server.operation.duration` attribute tables, where there are no spans. Signal-neutral wording reads correctly on both.

**It contradicts the note below.** The enumeration ("server-side error, timeout, or transport error") reads as exhaustive, but the note still says that when the JSON-RPC call succeeds and an error is returned inside the result payload (including `CallToolResult` with `isError: true`), `error.type` SHOULD be set to `tool_error` / the payload error. On a server span that isn't a server-side error, a timeout, or a transport error, so the two rules disagree about the most common MCP failure mode. Tool failures are server-side, so I'd fold them in:

```suggestion
          conditionally_required: >
            On the client side, if and only if the operation fails. On the server side,
            if and only if the operation fails with a server-side error, an error reported
            in the result payload, a timeout, or a transport error.
```

threads.body:
The classification only exists on the two span definitions, but the `error.type` note that points at it lives in `mcp.common.attributes`, which `mcp.operation.metrics.attributes` also references. In the generated `mcp.client.operation.duration` / `mcp.server.operation.duration` tables the result is a dangling reference: `error.type` says "See `rpc.response.status_code` for which error codes are considered server-side", while `rpc.response.status_code` still carries the generic upstream note ("Usually it represents an error code... Semantic conventions for individual RPC frameworks SHOULD document what `rpc.response.status_code` means..."). So `error.type` on `mcp.server.operation.duration` — the signal that most needs this rule — is unimplementable as written.

Can't express a cross-file suggestion, so concretely: move both overrides into shared internal groups in `model/mcp/common.yaml`, e.g.

```yaml
  - id: mcp.client.status.attributes
    visibility: internal
    attributes:
      - ref: rpc.response.status_code
        note: |
          All JSON-RPC error codes SHOULD be considered errors.

  - id: mcp.server.status.attributes
    visibility: internal
    attributes:
      - ref: rpc.response.status_code
        note: |
          <server-side classification>
```

then replace the inline overrides in `spans.yaml` with `- ref_group: mcp.client.status.attributes` / `- ref_group: mcp.server.status.attributes`, and reference the matching group from each metric in `model/mcp/metrics.yaml` (`mcp.operation.metrics.attributes` is shared by both metrics today, so either split it or add the `ref_group` per metric).

Separately, worth a second look at "all error codes" on the client: 2025-11-25 defines `-32042` (`URLElicitationRequiredError`), which tells the client to run a URL elicitation and retry. That's control flow, not a failure, and this rule turns it into an `ERROR` client span.

threads.body:
Two problems with this list.

**`-32002` is misclassified.** MCP tells servers to return `-32002` for "Resource not found" ([2025-11-25 `server/resources` → Error Handling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/resources#error-handling), same in 2025-06-18). It sits inside `-32000`..`-32099`, so this rule marks the MCP equivalent of an HTTP 404 as a server-side failure — the exact case the motivation says we want to stop flagging. Every `resources/read` for a URI the caller got wrong will set `error.type` and `ERROR` status on the server span and count as a failure in `mcp.server.operation.duration`.

**The allowlist is closed, so unrecognized codes default to "not an error".** MCP and SDKs define codes outside the `-3200x` block (2025-11-25 adds `-32042` `URLElicitationRequiredError`), and applications define their own. Under this rule a genuine server failure carrying a code the instrumentation doesn't recognize is silently recorded as success. HTTP defaults the other way: "any other code the client failed to interpret" is an error.

Inverting the list fixes both, and the excluded set becomes exactly the caller-fault codes:

```suggestion
      - ref: rpc.response.status_code
        note: |
          The following error codes indicate an error on the caller side and
          SHOULD NOT be considered errors:

          - `-32700` (`Parse error`)
          - `-32600` (`Invalid Request`)
          - `-32601` (`Method not found`)
          - `-32602` (`Invalid params`)
          - `-32002` ([`Resource not found`](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/resources#error-handling))

          Any other error code SHOULD be considered an error.
```

If you'd rather not blanket-classify unknown codes as errors, then at minimum `-32002` needs to come out of the server range, and the note should say what an instrumentation does with a code matching none of the listed ranges.
